I’m taking you beyond the red dunes to uncover 40 surprising facts that completely change how the Kalahari looks from the road.

I explore its underground water, ancient caves, salt pans, rivers, mines, trains, wildlife and remarkable landscapes—from the Eye of Kuruman and Dragon’s Breath Cave to the Okavango Delta and Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park.

I also look at San history and languages, diamond and manganese mining, the Kalahari’s extraordinary animals, and the climate threat that could set its fossil dunes moving again.
trascrizione_inizio: Did you know that a train almost 4 km long leaves the Kalahari every single day? And it's the longest production train on the planet. Or that a South African town literally named hottest hell holds most of the world's manganese and Tesla can't build its cars without it. How about the fact that under this so-called desert sits the largest underground lake ever found and nobody has touched the bottom? Well, there's a lot more to the Kalahari than red dunes and a sunset photo from Twee Rivieren. It looks empty from the N14. It is not empty. It is hiding some of the strangest geography on the African continent and most South Africans drive right past it on the way to Upington. Today, we're counting down 40 facts that will completely change how you see the Kalahari. Fact 40, the Kalahari is not actually a desert. A desert gets less than 250 mm of rain in a year. The driest corner of the Kalahari, down near the Botswana border, gets about 110 mm. But the northern and eastern parts get more than 500 mm, which is more rain than Cape Town sees in a normal year. The problem is the sand. Water hits the ground and vanishes straight down, so the surface looks bone dry an hour after a thunderstorm. The name says it all.
